subject: chem
title: Carbonyl Compounds
subtitle: Aldehydes, ketones and their reactions.
concept: Aldehydes (RCHO) and ketones (RCOR') both contain the C=O group; aldehydes can be oxidised to carboxylic acids, ketones cannot.
Nucleophilic addition is the characteristic reaction of carbonyl compounds — the δ+ carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.
2,4-DNPH forms an orange/yellow precipitate with all carbonyls; IR spectroscopy identifies C=O by a strong absorption at ~1700 cm⁻¹.

notes.heading: Aldehydes and Ketones
items: Both contain the C=O (carbonyl) group. In aldehydes, the carbonyl is at the end of the chain (–CHO); in ketones, it is within the chain (–CO–). Both show a strong, sharp IR absorption at ~1700–1750 cm⁻¹.

Test for any carbonyl: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH, Brady's reagent) — gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone. The melting point of the purified precipitate identifies the specific compound.
Distinguish aldehyde from ketone: Tollens' reagent (silver mirror = aldehyde); Fehling's/Benedict's (brick-red precipitate = aldehyde). Ketones do not react with either.

notes.heading: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions
items: The carbonyl carbon is δ+ (O is electronegative) — it is attacked by nucleophiles. Mechanism: nucleophile attacks the C=O carbon; the π bond breaks; O⁻ forms; then protonation gives the –OH product.
Reduction with NaBH₄ (sodium borohydride): H⁻ acts as the nucleophile. Aldehyde → primary alcohol; ketone → secondary alcohol.

Reaction with HCN (in presence of KCN catalyst): CN⁻ adds to the carbonyl → hydroxynitrile (contains –OH and –CN). The product has one more carbon than the original carbonyl compound, and a new chiral centre forms — equal amounts of both enantiomers are produced (racemic mixture).

definitions.body: A reaction in which a nucleophile adds across the C=O double bond; the π bond breaks and both atoms of the C=O gain a substituent.
2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine forms a yellow/orange precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone; the melting point of the precipitate identifies the specific compound.
Product of addition of HCN to an aldehyde or ketone; contains both –OH and –CN groups.

workedExamples.q: Describe the mechanism for the reaction of ethanal with HCN.

steps.text: CN⁻ (nucleophile) attacks the δ+ carbon of the C=O group, donating an electron pair.
The C=O π bond breaks; electrons move to O, forming O⁻.
O⁻ is protonated by H⁺ (from HCN) → product: CH₃CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile). A chiral centre is created.

mistakes: Using 2,4-DNPH to distinguish aldehyde from ketone — it reacts with both. Use Tollens' or Fehling's to distinguish.
Forgetting the chiral centre formed in HCN addition to an unsymmetrical aldehyde — equal amounts of both enantiomers (racemic mixture).
Stating NaBH₄ adds H₂ — it provides H⁻ ions as nucleophiles; not the same as catalytic hydrogenation.
tips: 2,4-DNPH tests FOR a carbonyl; Tollens'/Fehling's tests to distinguish aldehyde FROM ketone.
IR: C=O stretch appears as a strong, sharp absorption at ~1700–1750 cm⁻¹.
HCN addition: the product has a new chiral centre → forms a racemic mixture (50:50 enantiomers).

flashcards.a: Any carbonyl compound (aldehyde or ketone) — gives orange/yellow precipitate. Does NOT distinguish between them.

flashcards.q: How do you reduce a ketone to a secondary alcohol?
flashcards.a: React with NaBH₄ (sodium borohydride) in aqueous/ethanol solution — nucleophilic addition of H⁻.

flashcards.q: What functional groups does a hydroxynitrile contain?
What is the IR absorption for a C=O group?
flashcards.a: Strong, sharp absorption at approximately 1700–1750 cm⁻¹.

flashcards.q: Why is a racemic mixture formed when HCN adds to ethanal?
flashcards.a: CN⁻ can attack from either face of the planar C=O → equal amounts of R and S enantiomers (racemic mixture).

flashcards.q: Which carbonyl compounds react with Fehling's solution?
flashcards.a: Only aldehydes (they can be oxidised); ketones do not react.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces both aldehydes and ketones to alcohols?
questions.exp: NaBH₄ provides H⁻ as a nucleophile; it reduces C=O to C–OH in both aldehydes and ketones.

questions.q: What does a positive Tollens' test indicate?
questions.exp: Tollens' reagent oxidises aldehydes to carboxylates — a silver mirror forms. Ketones do not react.

questions.q: What is the product of HCN addition to propanone?
questions.exp: Propanone + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN = 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. Ketone + HCN adds to the carbonyl.

questions.q: Where does the IR absorption for C=O appear?
questions.exp: C=O stretching: strong sharp absorption at ~1700–1750 cm⁻¹ is characteristic of carbonyl compounds.

questions.q: 2,4-DNPH gives an orange precipitate with a compound. This confirms the presence of?
questions.exp: 2,4-DNPH reacts with all carbonyl compounds (both aldehydes and ketones) — it cannot distinguish between them.

recall: Describe the nucleophilic addition mechanism of HCN with an aldehyde.
Explain how to distinguish between an aldehyde and a ketone.
Describe the products of NaBH₄ reduction of an aldehyde and a ketone.
Explain why HCN addition to an unsymmetrical carbonyl gives a racemic mixture.
